title: Forty days from the top
hookLine: Moses forty days on the mountain, Jesus forty in the desert: the last forty
tomorrow: did Jesus tell stories to explain things, or to hide them?

lines: A NUMBER THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.
cards: Countdown apps love a round number. The Bible has one it keeps coming back to. The rain on Noah's ark falls forty days and forty nights.
Moses spends forty days on a mountain. Elijah walks forty days to one. Jesus spends forty in the desert.
Same number, four times, and the text never stops to explain it. So why forty? And why does this path have exactly forty days left, counting today?

teach.b: Start with what each forty holds. Exodus: Moses climbs into the cloud on Sinai, “and Moses was in the mount forty days and forty nights.” He comes down carrying the tables of stone.

Kings: Elijah is worn out, lying under a juniper tree, asking to die. An angel wakes him twice with bread and water, and he goes “in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God.”
Matthew: “Then was Jesus led up of the spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.”

Here's the pattern, and it's the answer to the puzzle. Each forty is a long in-between: long enough to be changed, and then it ends. Each ends with something new: a covenant, the law, a mountain, a ministry.
And nobody goes through it alone: Moses in the cloud, Elijah fed, Jesus led by the Spirit. Now the detail to tell a friend.

teach.h: THREE OF THEM ON ONE MOUNTAIN.
teach.b: Later in Matthew, Jesus takes three friends up a high mountain, and “there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.” Elias is Elijah. Two people of the forty days, standing with the third, on one mountain.
Churches that keep Lent tie its forty days to Jesus in the wilderness.
These last forty are gentler than a fast. They look back: the parables, Mary, the last week, the whole road, seen from near the top.

how: Churches that keep Lent observe a forty-day season before Easter of prayer, fasting and giving, linked to Jesus's forty days in the wilderness.

games.q: what does “forty days from the top” mean?
o: a forty-day fast required before the end
the forty lessons you can skip to finish
the path's last forty days, a final climb

p: rain for forty days and forty nights
in the mount, in the cloud

s: the Bible stops to explain why it uses the number forty
it never explains it. what each forty holds is the clue: a long in-between that ends.
in Matthew, Moses and Elijah appear on a mountain talking with Jesus
there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.
Jesus's forty days in the wilderness came right after his baptism
then was Jesus led up of the spirit into the wilderness.

games.q: your friend starts a forty-day phone-free challenge and quits on day nine, embarrassed. which detail from the forties fits best?
o: Elijah was ready to give up under a tree, was fed, and went on.
forty only counts if you finish it in one unbroken go.
the forties were meant to be done alone, with no help.
games.why: Elijah lay down asking to die. an angel woke him twice with bread and water, and he went in the strength of that meat forty days.

practice: Make a small plan for the forty days. Name, in a few words, what you hope they give you. Name the one thing most likely to get in the way, and decide now what you'll do when it does: a shorter version, a different hour.
If you pray, offer the forty days to God, then sit in the view.

wordCard.voice: Forty days from the top. The path's last forty days: a closing climb, in company, looking back over the whole road.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the last climb, forty days long enough to change something, and then they end. See you tomorrow.
